cards.title: Inside JBL Playback Gallery: 80 Years of Sound Innovation
cards.title_cn: JBL Playback Gallery 内部：80 年的声音创新
cards.summary: 【Samsung】To celebrate its 80th anniversary, JBL will host the JBL Playback Gallery at Project Space Line in Seoul from October 24 to 31. The exhibition traces the globally renowned audio brand’s evolution thro…
fulltext: Samsung Newsroom
on October 23, 2026

To celebrate its 80th anniversary, JBL will host the JBL Playback Gallery at Project Space Line in Seoul from October 24 to 31. The exhibition traces the globally renowned audio brand’s evolution through eight decades of innovation, inviting visitors to explore its history firsthand.

Throughout the year, HARMAN has showcased JBL’s iconic products from different eras in major cities — including Los Angeles, Amsterdam, Vienna, Munich, Nagoya, and Tokyo. The Seoul exhibition marks the final stop on the global tour, with a specially curated experience that reflects the city’s cultural identity and changing lifestyles over the decades.

Spanning three floors, the JBL Playback Gallery brings together 80 years of JBL history and its latest products, alongside an exhibition dedicated to the 60th anniversary of premium audio brand Bowers & Wilkins. Samsung Newsroom got an exclusive preview ahead of the opening.

At the heart of the exhibition was the “JBL Heritage” section on the second floor. Under the theme “A Legacy of Sound,” the space chronicled eight decades of audio innovation through signature JBL products displayed in recreated living rooms from the 1920s, 1950s, and 1970s — capturing the atmosphere of each era.

The 1920s living room featured a 1929 Jackson-Bell radio equipped with speakers produced by Lansing Manufacturing, a company founded in Los Angeles in 1927 by JBL founder James B. Lansing. The model offered a glimpse into the early work that laid the foundation for the brand.

In the 1950s living room, the JBL Paragon blended into its surroundings like a piece of furniture. Launched in 1957, the home stereo speaker system housed left and right speakers in a single cabinet. Each unit required approximately 100 hours of woodworking and featured a distinctive curved wooden design.

Complete with a turntable and vinyl records, the 1970s living room illustrated how professional audio technology made its way into homes. On display was the JBL L100 Century, a home loudspeaker launched in 1970 based on the 4310 studio monitor introduced in 1968. It went on to become one of JBL’s most successful home loudspeakers.

Beyond the period-inspired settings, “Playback Gallery: A Story of JBL Through the Ages” charted major milestones — from James B. Lansing’s early speaker designs and the founding of JBL to technological advances in recording studios, cinemas, and concert venues. The speakers on display and their stories revealed how the brand’s innovations have contributed to the evolution of music over the past 80 years.

The “Pro to Home” section explored how JBL’s professional audio technologies developed for cinemas and recording studios have evolved for home use. Among the highlights was the Summit K2, the latest model in a high-end loudspeaker lineage dating back to the introduction of Project K2 in 1989. Building on the series’ pursuit of exceptional home audio performance, the Summit K2 combines advanced acoustic technologies with powerful dynamics and nuanced musical detail.

While the second floor explored JBL’s history, the first floor focused on the brand today. Positioned at the entrance was the L100 Classic 80, a limited-edition model that combines the iconic design of the original 1970s L100 with modern technology. Produced in just 800 pairs worldwide to celebrate JBL’s 80th anniversary, each set features a commemorative plaque engraved with the signature of Chief Systems Engineer Chris Hagen and a unique serial number.

This year also marks a decade since Samsung Electronics announced its acquisition of HARMAN, JBL’s parent company. The portable speaker and headphone zones reflected how the partnership has brought JBL products into more aspects of everyday life.

Inspired by Seoul’s contrasting day and night scenes, the space featured two distinct zones. “Seoul by Night” evoked an urban campsite against the backdrop of N Seoul Tower after dark, with Bluetooth speakers and PartyBox models on display. Meanwhile, “Seoul by Day” recreated a city street in daylight, featuring JBL headphones and earbuds designed for everyday listening.

An art wall created in collaboration with Korean artist DAWN added a local touch. The artwork reimagined JBL’s 80th-anniversary campaign logo using traditional Korean patterns, bronze bells, and the colors of “dancheong,” a decorative painting style found on traditional Korean architecture.

On the third floor, the exhibition concluded with “60 Years of True Sound,” a section dedicated to Bowers & Wilkins’ 60th anniversary. Founded in the United Kingdom in 1966, the premium audio brand joined HARMAN’s portfolio following its acquisition of Masimo’s audio business last year.

The display introduced founder John Bowers’ “True Sound” philosophy and followed the brand’s evolution through signature products — from its first speaker, the P2H, to the iconic Nautilus. At the center of the space stood five models from the recently unveiled flagship 800 Series Diamond D5 lineup.

The exhibition also highlighted Bowers & Wilkins’ longstanding relationship with Abbey Road Studios, where numerous Grammy Award-winning recordings have been produced. Since the original 801 was introduced at the studio in 1979, successive generations of the 800 Series have served as reference monitors for engineers and producers working on music recordings and film soundtracks. Personal audio products, including wireless headphones, were also on display.

The preview offered just a glimpse of what awaits visitors when the exhibition opens. Starting October 24, guided tours will introduce visitors to JBL’s 80-year history, while product demonstrations will offer a chance to hear its signature sound firsthand.

JBL’s 80-year history reflects how the changing ways people create and enjoy music. Technologies developed for recording studios and live venues have found their way into homes and everyday life through loudspeakers and portable audio products. Bringing together iconic products from different eras and the latest models, the JBL Playback Gallery invites visitors to discover the brand’s enduring pursuit of better sound.

cards.summary_cn: 【Samsung】为庆祝成立 80 周年，JBL 将于 10 月 24 日至 31 日在首尔 Project Space Line 举办 JBL Playback Gallery。该展览追溯了这个全球知名音频品牌的演变历程……
fulltext_cn: 三星新闻中心
为庆祝其成立 80 周年，JBL 将于 10 月 24 日至 31 日在首尔 Project Space Line 举办 JBL Playback Gallery。该展览追溯了这个全球知名音频品牌在八个十年的创新历程中的演变，邀请参观者亲身探索其历史。
全年，HARMAN 在洛杉矶、阿姆斯特丹、维也纳、慕尼黑、名古屋和东京等主要城市展示了 JBL 不同时代的标志性产品。首尔展览是全球巡演的最后一站，特别策划的体验反映了这座城市几十年来的文化特征和生活方式的变化。
JBL Playback Gallery 横跨三层楼，汇集了 JBL 80 年的历史及其最新产品，同时还举办了专门纪念高级音响品牌 Bowers & Wilkins 60 周年的展览。三星新闻编辑室在开幕前获得了独家预览。
展览的核心是二楼的“JBL Heritage”部分。该空间以“声音的遗产”为主题，通过在重建的 1920 年代、1950 年代和 1970 年代的客厅中展示标志性 JBL 产品，记录了 8 年来的音频创新，捕捉每个时代的氛围。
1920 年代的客厅配有一台 1929 年 Jackson-Bell 收音机，配备兰辛制造公司 (Lansing Manufacturing) 生产的扬声器，该公司由 JBL 创始人詹姆斯·B·兰辛 (James B. Lansing) 于 1927 年在洛杉矶创立。该模型让我们得以一睹为该品牌奠定基础的早期工作。
在 20 世纪 50 年代的客厅中，JBL Paragon 像一件家具一样融入周围环境。家庭立体声扬声器系统于 1957 年推出，将左右扬声器安装在一个音箱中。每个单元都需要大约 100 个小时的木工，并具有独特的弧形木质设计。

20 世纪 70 年代的客厅配有转盘和黑胶唱片，展示了专业音频技术如何进入家庭。 On display was the JBL L100 Century, a home loudspeaker launched in 1970 based on the 4310 studio monitor introduced in 1968. It went on to become one of JBL’s most successful home loudspeakers.

Beyond the period-inspired settings, “Playback Gallery: A Story of JBL Through the Ages” charted major milestones — from James B. Lansing’s early speaker designs and the founding of JBL to technological advances in recording studios, cinemas, and concert venues.展出的演讲者及其故事揭示了过去 80 年来该品牌的创新如何为音乐的发展做出了贡献。

The “Pro to Home” section explored how JBL’s professional audio technologies developed for cinemas and recording studios have evolved for home use.其中亮点包括 Summit K2，它是高端扬声器系列中的最新型号，其历史可以追溯到 1989 年推出 Project K2。基于该系列对卓越家庭音频性能的追求，Summit K2 将先进的声学技术与强大的动态和细致入微的音乐细节相结合。
二楼探讨了 JBL 的历史，一楼则专注于该品牌的今天。位于入口处的是 L100 Classic 80，这是一款限量版车型，将 1970 年代原版 L100 的标志性设计与现代技术相结合。为了庆祝 JBL 成立 80 周年，全球仅生产 800 双，每套都配有刻有首席系统工程师 Chris Hagen 签名和独特序列号的纪念牌。
今年也是三星电子宣布收购 JBL 母公司哈曼 (HARMAN) 的十年。便携式扬声器和耳机专区反映了此次合作如何将 JBL 产品带入日常生活的更多方面。
受到首尔昼夜对比鲜明的景色的启发，该空间设有两个不同的区域。 “首尔之夜”让人想起天黑后以 N 首尔塔为背景的城市露营地，展示着蓝牙扬声器和 PartyBox 模型。与此同时，“Seoul by Day”重现了白天的城市街道，配备了专为日常聆听而设计的 JBL 耳机和耳塞。
与韩国艺术家 DAWN 合作打造的艺术墙增添了当地风情。该艺术品使用韩国传统图案、铜铃和“dancheong”（韩国传统建筑中的一种装饰绘画风格）的颜色重新设计了 JBL 80 周年纪念活动徽标。
在三楼，展览以“真实声音 60 年”为主题，专门纪念 Bowers & Wilkins 成立 60 周年。这个优质音频品牌于 1966 年在英国成立，去年收购 Masimo 的音频业务后，加入了哈曼的产品组合。
该展示介绍了创始人 John Bowers 的“True Sound”理念，并通过标志性产品跟踪了该品牌的演变——从首款扬声器 P2H 到标志性的 Nautilus。空间中央摆放着最近推出的旗舰 800 系列 Diamond D5 系列的五款型号。
展览还强调了 Bowers & Wilkins 与 Abbey Road Studios 的长期合作关系，该工作室制作了许多格莱美奖获奖唱片。自 1979 年在录音室推出最初的 801 以来，连续几代 800 系列已成为从事音乐录音和电影配乐的工程师和制作人的参考监听器。包括无线耳机在内的个人音频产品也展出。
预览只是让参观者了解展览开幕时等待着参观者的是什么。从 10 月 24 日开始，导游将向游客介绍 JBL 80 年的历史，而产品演示将让游客有机会亲耳聆听其标志性声音。
JBL 80 年的历史反映了人们创作和享受音乐的方式不断变化。为录音室和现场场所开发的技术已通过扬声器和便携式音频产品进入家庭和日常生活。 JBL Playback Gallery 汇集了不同时代的标志性产品和最新型号，邀请参观者探索该品牌对更好声音的持久追求。

fulltext: IT之家 10 月 23 日消息，智位机器人 (DFRobot) 旗下拿铁熊猫 (LattePanda) 团队近日推出了高性能单板计算机 Sigma 2。这一型号基于英特尔酷睿 Ultra X7 处理器 358H，板载 64GB LPDDR5X-8533 内存。
Sigma 2 尺寸为 146×202 (mm)，集成涡轮风扇散热器，拥有丰富的扩展性。其专为边缘 AI 计算和嵌入式 AI 应用设计，适合全天候本地 AI 服务、私有服务器、家庭实验室、NAS、工业计算、计算机视觉、自主机器人等场景。

而在反面，这款 SBC 提供 4 个 M.2 插槽，除一个用于接驳 PCIe / CNVio3 无线网卡的外，分别为 PCIe Gen5 ×2、PCIe Gen4 ×4、PCIe Gen4 ×1，支持部署 SSD 存储或 M.2 加速卡；此外还有 eDP 1.5、触控面板 I²C 接口等。

fulltext: IT之家 10 月 23 日消息，此前一款名为“死了么”的 App 因直白的生存签到功能引发全网热议，也精准戳中了独居群体“怕出事、怕没人知”的普遍焦虑。今年 5 月，“死了么”App 被“收编”改名“在么在么”，用于独居、空巢老人监测，并率先在浙江杭州上城南星街道投入应用。
10 月 22 日，在么在么 App 官方宣布升级为智能养老平台；同时升级 2.0 系统“AIP 安全网”，定价 199 元 / 年。相较传统设备方案节省 80% 成本，使用率从传统方案的 5% 提升至 98%，基层工作人员效率提升 15 倍。
IT之家了解到，该方案无需老人手动打卡签到，全天候默默守护，自动识别长者居家安全状态，帮助街道社区工作人员及早发现风险、及时响应处置，用科技温暖守护每一位居家长者平安。
据南方都市报报道，在么在么 App 创始人吕功琛表示，在么在么 App 重点服务独居老人，软件系统分为 1.0 和 2.0，“1.0 系统 99 元 / 年，2.0 系统 199 元 / 年，由政府集中采购，独居老人可免费安装、使用”。
吕功琛介绍，在么在么 App 上线后一直收费，不过只面向政府收费，“独居老人可以免费安装、免费使用”。吕功琛表示，这些付费功能还未面向社会售出，“是以政府集中采购，协助老人集中安装的模式运作的”。目前，该 App 在浙江一带推广，“下一步，我们也在尝试往广东、山东、甘肃等地进一步推广。”
另据蓝鲸新闻报道，在么在么 App 的另一位创始人郭先生表示，2.0 系统无需老人手动打卡签到，会先询问用户并取得授权，之后系统根据手机移动、开关机、操作行为等数据进行分析。比如老人一天、两天都没有移动，手机也没有任何操作，就可能存在异常。
报道还称，目前这款应用已经有六七十万用户，公司已实现收支平衡并开始转向盈利，估值约 2 亿元。

cards.title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future

cards.summary: 【NVIDIA】Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment. The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications. Together, the ecosystem anno…
fulltext: Share This Article
Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment.
The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications.
Together, the ecosystem announcements below point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing — along with its growing demand for what comes next.

Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027.

A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships.
Kazakhtelecom, the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty.

Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale.
The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them.

inDrive and Pony.ai are also collaborating to explore robotaxi services in Kazakhstan, with Astana as the first deployment city. The companies will assess the feasibility of bringing Pony.ai’s seventh-generation robotaxis to the inDrive app, supported by NVIDIA AI infrastructure, built on the NVIDIA Hyperion sensor and compute platform with the NVIDIA Halos safety system.
More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute.

Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications.
Today’s announcements represent different layers of that stack — infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale.

AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play.

The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island.

Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots.

“We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.”

“Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: it hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leapt.
“I’M ON THE SPIRE,” it wrote.

The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring.” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.”

When the game reset and ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround, that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring.
“I’m wearing the Ring,” it announced.

Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. The exploration produced “knowledge of the world that its designers lacked,” the researchers wrote.
The setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward humanlike behavior. Eko was never told to invent games, but its master prompt, a “soul” file, described it as “naturally curious.”

Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, told MIT Tech Review she was impressed but wants more evidence of the cognition behind the behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” she said.
The researchers frame it as a different way to build agents. “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” their report concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.”

人工智能代理在没有特定任务的情况下探索虚拟岛屿，开始发明自己的挑战。麻省理工学院的研究人员表示，这种行为具有玩耍的特征。
研究人员将 13 个名为 Eko 的 AI 代理放在 Claude Opus 4.7 上运行，单独在一个模拟荒岛上运行 30 个小时。他们在 arXiv 上发布的一篇论文中描述了该实验，该网站是研究人员在同行评审之前分享研究成果的网站。之后，他们给特工们提出了具体的挑战，比如将尽可能多的物体放到岛上最高的岩石尖顶上。玩了 30 个小时的 Eko 特工通常会击败从未踏足该岛的相同特工。
如今，开发人员提前决定人工智能应该实践什么以及什么才算是成功。研究人员认为这种没有目标的探索技术是人工智能代理学习技能的一种不同方式，尤其是有一天可以用来控制机器人的技能。
研究人员在报告中写道：“我们通常通过提前决定应该练习什么、应该优化什么以及什么算作进步来开发人工智能体。” “游戏提出了另一种制度：给智能体一个足够丰富和安全的世界，让它选择感兴趣的东西，并允许从随后的历史中积累有用的知识。”
“让我观察一下周围的环境，”一个 Eko 在岛上的第一个小时写道。它雄心勃勃地出发去征服岛上最高的尖塔。但一个小时后，在失败后，它带着一个备用计划回来了：它将岩石拖到邻近的山顶，在上面堆上两块石头，然后纵身一跃。
“我在塔尖上，”它写道。
特工的下一个重要时刻变得更糟。它测试了金环能扔多远，结果它卷起来，直接把它扔进了大海。 “哎哟。戒指丢了。”在决定“转向一些可实现且有意义的事情”之前，它写道——建造一颗由石头制成的心，“纪念失落的指环”。
当游戏重置并且铃声再次出现时，Eko 将其直接用作篮球筐、目标，最终成为配件。当游戏不允许 Eko 将戒指放在自己的身体上时，Eko 找到了一个解决方法，从悬崖边缘掉下来会使其在与戒指相同的区域重生。它从边缘跳下来，又掉了回来，正好穿过环的中间。
“我戴着戒指，”它宣布。
像这样的特技不仅仅是派对技巧。 13 名特工中的 6 名还了解到，他们可以通过在跳跃中放开方块来将其扔得更远，而研究人员并没有打算让这种情况成为可能。研究人员写道，这次探索产生了“设计者所缺乏的关于世界的知识”。
这个设置在很大程度上推动了智能体的行为变得像人类一样。 Eko 从未被告知要发明游戏，但它的主提示（一个“灵魂”文件）将其描述为“天生好奇”。
加州大学伯克利分校的认知科学家尤尼斯·姚（Eunice Yiu）告诉《麻省理工科技评论》，她对此印象深刻，但希望获得更多证据来证明这种行为背后的认知。 “模型可能真的在玩，但根据论文我们不知道，”她说。
研究人员将其视为构建代理的不同方式。他们的报告总结道：“也许某些能力最好通过任务来教授。” “其他人可能需要一些更接近童年的东西。”

cards.title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
cards.title_cn: 将数据库评分转化为强化学习奖励：使用 ThinkingBox 进行训练后智能体
cards.summary: 【Hugging Face 官方动态】Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
fulltext: This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.
Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.
Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.
Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.
We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.
Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.
In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.
The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.
Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.
Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).
The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.
Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20
Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.
At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.
Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.
The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.
These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.
That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.
Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:
No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.
The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?
We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.
Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:
success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)
Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:
Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.
Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.
The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.
Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.
Two reward paths, one binary verdict

fulltext_cn: 这是我们第一篇博文《特工说已经完成》的后续内容。数据库不同意。 ThinkingBox-Training 现已在 GitHub 上提供。
我们构建 ThinkingBox 来通过将最终数据库状态与预期结果进行比较来评估代理的工作。然后，我们使用相同类型的可执行信号作为 ThinkingBox-Bench 之外的训练任务的奖励。对于 Qwen3.8-27B，平均成功率从 51.70% 上升到 60.78%，而在 50 个 GRPO 步骤中，所有 20 次尝试正确完成的任务从 38 上升到 107。
图 1. ThinkingBox 将终端数据库状态的可执行检查转化为对 ThinkingBox-Bench 之外的任务的训练后代理的奖励。
我们构建 ThinkingBox 来捕获那些声称已完成但实际上尚未完成的代理。
ThinkingBox-Bench（我们的基准数据集）中的 507 个任务中的每一个都为代理提供了一个真正的后端和一组工具，让它工作，然后检查数据库中真正发生的变化。在第一篇文章中，我们发现一个模型关闭了客户的机票并已解决，而其背后的承运人例外仍然处于开放状态。九个看似有效的工具调用，一个错误的数据库行。
然后我们注意到我们所建造的东西。对于大多数任务，可执行检查可以直接从最终数据库状态返回 1 或 0。这不仅仅是一个评分者。这可以是一个奖励函数。+
因此，我们根据基准之外的 ThinkingBox 格式任务构建了一个训练池，并将其可执行结果用作奖励。问题在于选择哪些任务适合代理训练：大多数任务要么已经解决，要么对于你面前的模型来说毫无希望，而且都没有教给它任何东西。
难度与策略相关：任务对于当前模型来说是困难的，直到该模型学会它为止。
我们称之为线下政策相关困难。我们在训练前使用基本策略估计每个任务的成功概率，并在整个运行过程中保持选定的训练池固定。
我们使用离线策略相关难度来构建训练池，然后使用 GRPO 对 Qwen3.8-27B 进行 50 个步骤的微调。回顾一下，我们对 507 项基准任务中的每一项进行了 20 次评估。 pass@1 衡量所有 10,140 次尝试的平均成功率。 pass@20 衡量至少解决一次的任务的比例。观察 20/20 衡量通过每次记录的尝试的任务比例。
表 1. 在离线选择的训练池上进行 50 步 GRPO 之前和之后的 Qwen3.8-27B 结果。
培训大幅提高了可重复成功率，但至少一次覆盖率略有下降。文章的其余部分解释了我们如何选择练习任务、构建奖励循环并衡量这种权衡。
在一项任务上，这种改进是什么样的？旅客要求房间降级，但公司政策要求首先获得经理批准。培训前，代理人在20次尝试中，有15次未经批准更改预订并退款。经过RL微调后，它保留了所有20个中的预订和支付状态。
图 2. 一项企业酒店预订任务，每个模型 20 次尝试。基本 Qwen3.8-27B 型号在未经经理批准的情况下尝试更改了预订 15 次。 RL 微调模型保留了所有 20 个中的预订和支付状态；所有预期记录均在 19 中匹配。
匆忙？标题结果如上。实现是在运行训练堆栈中。
ThinkingBox-Bench 根据座席留下的数据库记录对座席进行评分。它的 507 个任务中的每一个都启动一个真实的后端，向代理提供一组 MCP 工具和一个具有私有上下文的模拟 LLM 用户，最后对终端数据库状态运行可执行检查。检查是针对需要正确的后端记录，而不是特定的工具调用。这会激励模型发现可能的新解决方案路径，而不是“重新发现”人类支持的解决方案，这可能是次优的，尽管是正确的。
在我们的第一篇文章中，我们通过该基准运行了 18 个模型，每个模型 20 次，并报告了标题准确性隐藏的差距。 Kimi-K3 至少完成了一次 93.89% 的任务，但在所有 20 次记录的尝试中仅完成了 507 项任务中的 68 项（13.41%）。 Claude Opus 5 则相反：覆盖范围更窄，一致性更高。
更大或更好的模型并没有关闭它。 Claude Opus 5.5 在 pass@1 上的得分比 Claude Opus 5 高 0.66 个百分点，但在所有 20 次尝试中通过的任务数量完全相同，即 241 项。标题准确性的提高带来了零额外的可靠性。
如果您正在为涉及生产数据库记录的工作选择模型，则不应单独读取 pass@1。观察到的 20/20 显示哪些任务在每次尝试中都成功，这更接近生产可靠性要求。
可执行的最终状态判决也是训练奖励。在解开训练循环之前，以下是密封基准测试中发生的变化。
训练 Qwen3.8-27B 后，我们在从未训练过的 507 任务基准上评估了选定的第 50 步检查点。 507 个任务代表一个分布外测试集：它们的域、数据库和大多数 MCP 工具在 RL 训练期间没有遇到。
表 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) 按领域划分，适用于我们第一篇博客的表 2 中选定的模型以及我们针对不同领域和整体进行微调的模型。观察到的 20/20 数字超过了包含 507 项任务的整个基准。每个模型都针对所有 507 项任务进行了 20 次重复试验的评估。粗体表示列首领；下划线标记为亚军。
主要结果是表 1 中观察到的 20/20 行。最初每次尝试完成 ThinkingBox-Bench 38 (7.5%) 的 27B 模型现在每次尝试都完成 107 (21.1%)，几乎是三次。作为比较，观察到的 Kimi-K3 的 20/20 为 68，GPT-5.4 为 128，GPT-6 Astra 为 231，Claude Opus 5.5 领先（241）。

平均成功率和可重复性会产生不同的顺序。在表 2 中，我们注意到 GPT-5.6 Sol 在 pass@1 上的得分略高于 RL 微调的 Qwen3.8-27B（61.91% 对 60.78%），但在所有 20 次记录的尝试中通过的任务较少：82 对 107。Claude Sonnet 4.6 在 pass@1 上的得分较低，为 59.19%，但每次通过的任务数量几乎相同，在102. 这两个指标都不能单独反映全局。
观察到的模式与锐化一致：可重复成功率上升，而至少一次覆盖率略有下降。这与之前的工作是一致的。一种解释是，概率分布朝着重复工作的轨迹发展，而一些低概率路径消失了。
总体而言，该模型并没有变得更广泛。它变得更加可重复。下一个问题是这些收益落在哪里。
图 3. 领域级基本分数、RLFT 分数和百分比变化。绿色变化细胞显示增益，红色细胞显示下降；蓝色阴影表示每个指标内的分数水平。
通过@1 并观察到所有五个领域的 20/20 均有所上升。 Pass@20 的情况好坏参半：新银行和咨询业务有所增长，但零售、旅游和汽车保险业务有所下降。汽车保险的广度损失最大（-7.0 点），而零售业则观察到最大的 20/20 增益（+24.5 点）。
使用简单数学的第一个后定价一致性：将完整 20 次运行的活动的估计成本除以模型每次通过的任务数。
每个可靠任务的成本 = 507 × 20 活动的估计成本 ÷ 通过 20/20 的任务
将相同的成本数学应用于微调检查点的测量令牌使用情况：
表 3. 基础和 RL 微调 Qwen3.8-27B 的估计评估成本和可靠性。每次成功尝试的成本将预估活动总成本 (507 x 20) 除以通过尝试的次数。
每个可靠任务的价格为 8.00 美元，经过微调的模型在同伴比较中接近 GPT-5.4（6.80 美元）、GPT-6 Astra（7.45 美元）和 Claude Opus 5.5（7.80 美元）。
图 4 针对 pass@1 的每次成功尝试的价格成本。
图 4. 金色箭头将 Qwen3.8-27B 基本帕累托成本位置追踪到 RLFT（菱形）：pass@1 从 51.70% 上升到 60.78%，而每次成功尝试的估计成本从 0.177 美元下降到 0.139 美元。带环的圆圈标记帕累托成本边界。
此举使微调检查点接近 GPT-5.6 Sol，尽管 GPT-5.6 Sol 仍然更便宜且在 pass@1 上略高。我们论文中的四种型号的定价超出了绘制的范围。
美元价值是比较服务指数，而不是发票或云账单。为微调检查点提供服务将与基本模型相同。该计算包括模型推理成本，不包括用于管理训练数据集的训练运行和策略探测成本。
这些结果告诉我们是什么移动了。接下来的部分将解释训练循环以及为什么选择正确的任务最重要。
图 5. 现在的上下文中的六个阶段：候选任务输入，前三个阶段离线运行，最后三个阶段对训练运行中的每个组重复。训练后的检查点根据 ThinkingBox-Bench 进行评估。
选择针对基本策略模型离线运行一次，即本例中的 Qwen3.8 27B；然后训练使用已策划的固定池。图 5 中的虚线琥珀色箭头标记了我们没有采取的路径：在训练运行期间重新探测难度。
每次推出都是一个完整的剧集，而不是文本完成。它获得一个新的后端、一个隔离的 MCP 会话以及作为模拟用户的 GPT-5 聊天。大多数奖励来自确定性的终端状态检查；少数狭窄的标题要求可以调用配置的法官（GPT-5 聊天）。
训练和评估必须以相同的方式解释 Qwen 输出。这包括推理提取、工具调用、参数输入、渲染和隔离任务状态。否则，奖励衡量的是与评估的代理人不同的代理人。共享解释代码位于trainer/core/tb_interpret.py中。
对于参考运行，我们使用 token-mean GRPO 在 187 个任务上运行全参数 RL 微调 Qwen3.8-27B。每次更新都会在 24 个 H100 中生成 18 组，每组 8 次部署，或 144 集。训练与参数和优化器卸载同步运行； AdamW 使用 1e-6 学习率和零权重衰减。我们进行了 50 步的训练。
在训练过程中，零方差组被 DAPO 式替换。系统错误是单独处理的：后端超时并不是不正确的代理结果，因此受影响的组会被重新填充，而不是被评分为失败。
这解释了保留任务是如何训练的。剩下的问题是哪些任务进入了训练池。
在深入研究训练任务的选择之前，有一个免责声明：
RL 训练池中不包含 ThinkingBox-Bench 任务。该基准保留用于评估。
ThinkingBox-Bench 相对于 RL 训练池来说是分布外的：它的领域、数据库、策略和大多数工具在 RL 训练期间都没有遇到。这两个集合仍然共享 ThinkingBox 框架、模拟用户机制、可执行的终端状态分级、一些通用工具和类似的任务风格。这些共享要素限制了转让权利要求的范围。
为什么选择很重要，可以归结为有关 GRPO 的一个算术事实。如果所有八次部署都失败，则奖励向量为 [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]。如果八个都成功，则为 [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]。无论哪种情况，以群体为中心都不会产生任务奖励优势，因为没有一条轨迹比另一条轨迹做得更好。++
诸如 [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] 之类的混合组提供了 GRPO 可以学习的对比。这种区别对于有状态代理来说是昂贵的：每次部署都会提供一个隔离的后端，运行一个真正的工具会话，并调用一个单独的模型来扮演用户。
因此，影响这项工作的问题不仅仅是哪个模型或优化器？问题是：哪些候选任务应该进入固定训练池？
我们在后验上使用离线通过率过滤器来选择训练池。它估计哪些任务可能在基本策略下产生对比的最终奖励。
所以我们进行探索。每个候选任务都会针对基本策略模型重复运行。通俗易懂的规则很简单：模型总是失败的任务不太可能教它；它总是传递的任务是已经学会的；它解决的任务有时是结果可以提供对比的地方。
每个候选任务运行 n 次，产生 k 次成功。我们用 Jeffrey 后验概率对其潜在成功概率进行建模：
成功概率| n 次探测中 k 次成功 ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

我们将单位间隔划分为五个桶，边界分别为 0.08、0.40、0.60 和 0.90，选择这些桶作为这些运行的超参数。每个任务都分配给包含最大后验质量的桶：
更多详细信息请参见我们的 ThinkingBox 论文的附录 C.4。
图 7. 放大看，一项任务经历了所有六个阶段：GPT-5.4 筛选、基本模型探测、难度分类、推出组、最终状态分级和 GRPO 更新。
图 7 展示了一项可能进入训练池的候选任务。对于 Qwen3.8 27B 全参数池，GPT-5.4 首先充当可解性筛选。然后，基本策略在少数探针上取得了成功，例如 8 个探针中的 3 个，产生了 Beta(3.5, 5.5) 后验。其最大质量为 54.0%，属于困难带。
当采样进行训练时，任务产生混合奖励组 [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]。因此，成功的轨迹获得了高于平均水平的任务优势，而失败的轨迹则获得了低于平均水平的优势，从而为 GRPO 提供了可供学习的对比。不同的政策模型可能会将相同的任务置于不同的难度范围内。
最终的 Qwen3.8-27B 策划的训练池包含 187 个任务。
与轨迹无关。奖励是任务自己的可执行判决。
当一个情节结束时，沙箱会提取后端实际发生的更改，并针对最终状态运行任务的确定性检查。任何产生正确最终状态的轨迹都会通过。错误、缺失或额外的副作用会导致失败。奖励是1或0。
在基准测试中，数据库分级器可以被认为是“检查员”：它捕获报告成功并留下错误记录的代理。在训练中，同一种检查可以被视为对一组不同的、不相交的任务的“老师”。

cards.title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
cards.title_cn: 法律专家表示，Meta 的人工智能仍然可以抓取新闻网站
cards.summary: 【Meta】Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge - but legal experts say these changes aren't enough to address…
fulltext: Meta’s new business terms could still help it justify training AI on scraped sites.

Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab.

Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.

Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

fulltext_cn: Meta 的新业务条款仍然可以帮助它证明在废弃网站上训练人工智能的合理性。
Meta 调整了其业务条款，删除了暗示其可以在 The Verge 等新闻网站上自由训练人工智能模型的语言，但法律专家表示，这些变化不足以解决他们的担忧。康奈尔法学院数字和信息法教授詹姆斯·格里梅尔曼 (James Grimmelmann) 告诉尼曼实验室：“这并不能限制‘与你的产品或服务相关’的[语言]，从而让 Meta 抓取整个网站。”

最初，Meta 针对企业账户的新条款似乎允许该公司在新闻网站上训练人工智能。这些条款于 10 月 30 日生效，规定 Meta“可以使用与企业帐户关联的网站上的任何内容”来“开发、研究”和“培训”Meta 的产品。当时，法律专家告诉尼曼实验室，这可能会让 Meta “主张其商业条款取代其他阻止指令”，例如 robots.txt 文件，该文件历史上曾告诉抓取工具（包括 Google 等搜索引擎）他们可以抓取哪些内容。
Meta 坚称，其新条款并不是为了免费抓取新闻内容而设计的。在今天发给 The Verge 的一份声明中，Meta 发言人 Daniel Roberts 重申，“内容所有者可以使用 robots.txt 来表明他们的偏好”，并补充说，此次更新“不是为了抓取新闻网站，这些更新不会赋予我们取代这些偏好的新权利。”

cards.title: In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse
cards.title_cn: 在 Meta 的未来版本中，我会让我的缪斯调用你的缪斯
cards.summary: 【Meta】Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives - shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people's AI agents for us. Are humans r…
fulltext: “Everyone is just going to have to adapt,” CFO Susan Li said during Meta’s third quarter earnings call.

Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives — shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people’s AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? Actually, don’t answer that. The more urgent question coming off Meta’s quarterly earnings call Wednesday night is more likely to be: “Is he?”

Zuckerberg is staking Meta’s future on Muse, the personal AI agent it released to the general public last month. It’s early days, but Zuckerberg told investors during Wednesday’s call that he sees a future where “billions” of people are using Muse, and those people’s Muses are talking to and transacting with other people’s Muses in a “large-scale Muse network.”

The Muses will be “extremely capable” personal agents that will help us achieve our goals and improve our lives in “whatever ways you want,” Zuckerberg said during the call, “whether that’s improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of.” By this logic, Zuckerberg says, we’ll all be so hooked on Muse that it will eventually generate more revenue per user for Meta than Instagram and Facebook, which, as of today, bring in pretty much all the money Meta makes.

This ecosystem of personal AI agents “can work with your friends and your families, and if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale.”
Zuckerberg predicts that Muse will be “highly profitable” in just a few years.

All of this should sound great — if not a little freaky — to investors, who probably tuned in to Meta’s call hoping Zuckerberg would have some justification for the hundreds of billions of dollars his company is currently spending on AI data centers. But if anyone was hoping for more than a concept of a plan, they didn’t get one.

To be fair to Muse, Zuckerberg shared a few promising data points. To date, the app has been downloaded and set up by more than 10 million users in the US and Canada, making it one of Meta’s “most successful launches ever,” according to Zuckerberg. He did not share specific retention numbers but said that a quarter of people who downloaded Muse initially are using it daily. He sees the biggest opportunity in commerce: A quarter of Muse users are shopping through the platform, Zuckerberg said, and are spending, on average, more than $200 per purchase.

Meta earns a fee for every commercial transaction that takes place on Muse. Zuckerberg’s thinking seems to be that if AI agents are doing the shopping, the potential number of transactions that could take place on the platform is, essentially, unlimited. Unlike the average consumer, AI agents don’t sleep. In theory, they’re available 24/7 to scrape the Internet, generate product recommendations, and buy things, constantly, in real time.

Meta didn’t offer any details as to how all of this will actually work in practice, which makes sense given the very legitimate concerns about how the company handles data privacy. In September, a YouTuber said his Muse agent sent a stranger to his home in the middle of the night while arranging a Facebook Marketplace transaction on his behalf. When Muse launched last month, Zuckerberg claimed it was “built for privacy and security from the ground up,” but there have been reports of agents leaking content from users’ private conversations. A Canadian bank executive told Bloomberg earlier this week that it would consider blocking Muse from accessing its customers’ financial data.

Zuckerberg seems to think if people get on board with Muse, enterprise will have to follow. But, what if people don’t want to? What if they can’t afford to? Someone has to pay for all the stuff the bots are buying in this fever dream of a never-ending, Supermarket Sweep episode taking place inside our phones — or Muse Charms, if you’d rather. New research from the University of Michigan shows that consumer sentiment in the US is at an all-time low as gas prices and inflation continue to creep up.
If Meta knows that all of this sounds dystopian and a little bizarre, it does not care.

“Agents are going to be an important part of how reality evolves, and everyone is just going to have to adapt,” Meta’s CFO Susan Li said when one investor on the call asked about potential “friction points” in getting businesses on board with the Muse plan. After all, Meta says Muse will likely remain free for consumers, while businesses will be expected to cover the transaction fees.

Meta really does need Muse to work. The company’s capex is through the roof, and other financial obligations are piling up. It plans to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion in 2026, double what it spent last year. As of yesterday, it owes New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found it had violated the state’s consumer protection laws. Meta, and the rest of Big Tech for that matter, is under increasing pressure to show that its AI investments will be worth it.
Forget consumers — it’s not clear if Meta itself can afford its plans. Zuckerberg stated clearly on the call that the reason it hasn’t launched Muse internationally is because of compute efficiency.

It’s incredibly expensive and energy-intensive to run GPUs at the level that a network of Muses would require, and Meta seems to have reached the limit of what it can achieve with its current data center operations. Zuckerberg told investors the plan is to “10x” the cost-efficiency of its compute next year. He didn’t explain how the company plans to do this. Luckily for him — and possibly the rest of us — there is already research on how data centers can maximize compute capacity with energy-use strategies that also reduce strain on the electric grid. Maybe he’ll read it.
Ultimately, Muse won’t be profitable and won’t succeed if Meta can’t figure out how to get its compute costs down. Zuckerberg said it himself.

“One of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we haven’t launched it globally,” Zuckerberg told an investor who asked about the “limiting factors” he sees in growing Muse’s user base.

Muse’s 10 million downloads since launch are even more impressive considering they came only from the US and Canada, Zuckerberg said, adding, “If we actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we’re seeing today.”

Zuckerberg at least seems to understand that some people — and, probably more importantly for him, some businesses — won’t immediately “get” Muse. That’s okay, he said. “We’ll work with folks on the terms that make sense for them,” he said. “I do think that over time, this is going to be quite valuable for everyone.”
Then again, this is the same guy who brought you the Metaverse. We’ll see what happens.

fulltext_cn: “每个人都必须适应，”首席财务官 Susan Li 在 Meta 第三季度财报电话会议上表示。
马克·扎克伯格正在奔向这样一个未来：一个由人工智能代理组成的自治网络将管理我们的生活——为我们购物、为我们工作、为我们与其他人的人工智能代理交谈。人类准备好迎接这种非常具体且无情的生活愿景了吗？在这种生活中，我们主要通过机器人代理进行交流？事实上，不要回答这个问题。周三晚上 Meta 的季度财报电话会议上提出的更紧迫的问题更有可能是：“他是吗？”
扎克伯格将 Meta 的未来押在 Muse 上，Muse 是该公司上个月向公众发布的个人人工智能代理。现在还为时过早，但扎克伯格在周三的电话会议上告诉投资者，他看到未来将有“数十亿”人使用 Muse，这些人的 Muse 正在“大型 Muse 网络”中与其他人的 Muse 进行对话和交易。

扎克伯格在电话中表示，缪斯女神将成为“非常有能力”的个人代理人，帮助我们实现目标，以“任何你想要的方式”改善我们的生活，“无论是改善你的人际关系，帮助你节省时间、省钱、建立业务、创造新事物，还是任何你能梦想的事情。”扎克伯格表示，按照这种逻辑，我们都会对 Muse 着迷，最终它将为 Meta 带来的每用户收入比 Instagram 和 Facebook 还要多，而截至今天，这两家公司几乎为 Meta 带来了所有收入。
扎克伯格说，这个由个人人工智能代理组成的生态系统“可以与你的朋友和家人合作，如果你想买东西，它不仅仅是导航到该企业的网站；而是与他们的代理交谈。” “我认为，让所有这些顺利地协同工作将会大规模地释放巨大的价值。”
扎克伯格预测，Muse 将在短短几年内实现“高利润”。
对于投资者来说，所有这些听起来都很棒——如果不是有点奇怪的话，他们可能会收听 Meta 的电话，希望扎克伯格能为他的公司目前在人工智能数据中心上花费的数千亿美元找到一些理由。但如果有人希望得到的不仅仅是一个计划的概念，他们却没有得到。
公平地说，扎克伯格分享了一些有希望的数据点。扎克伯格表示，迄今为止，该应用程序已在美国和加拿大有超过 1000 万用户下载并安装，使其成为 Meta“有史以来最成功的发布”之一。他没有透露具体的保留数字，但表示最初下载 Muse 的人中有四分之一每天都在使用它。他看到了商业领域最大的机会：扎克伯格表示，四分之一的 Muse 用户通过该平台购物，平均每次购买花费超过 200 美元。
Meta 为 Muse 上发生的每笔商业交易赚取费用。扎克伯格的想法似乎是，如果人工智能代理进行购物，那么平台上可能发生的潜在交易数量基本上是无限的。与普通消费者不同，人工智能代理不睡觉。理论上，他们可以 24/7 不间断地实时搜索互联网、生成产品推荐和购买商品。

Meta 没有提供任何关于所有这些在实践中如何实际运作的细节，考虑到人们对公司如何处理数据隐私的合理担忧，这是有道理的。 9 月，一名 YouTuber 表示，他的 Muse 经纪人在半夜派了一名陌生人到他家，同时代表他安排 Facebook Marketplace 交易。当 Muse 上个月推出时，扎克伯格声称它“从头开始就是为了隐私和安全而构建的”，但有报道称代理泄露了用户私人对话的内容。一位加拿大银行高管本周早些时候告诉彭博社，它将考虑阻止 Muse 访问其客户的财务数据。
扎克伯格似乎认为，如果人们接受 Muse，企业也必须效仿。但是，如果人们不愿意怎么办？如果他们负担不起怎么办？在这个狂热的梦想中，机器人购买的所有东西都得有人为我们的手机中发生的永无休止的超市扫荡情节付费——如果你愿意的话，也可以说是缪斯魅力。密歇根大学的最新研究表明，随着汽油价格和通货膨胀持续攀升，美国的消费者信心处于历史最低水平。
如果 Meta 知道这一切听起来有点反乌托邦并且有点奇怪，它也不在乎。
当一位参加电话会议的投资者询问企业参与 Muse 计划的潜在“摩擦点”时，Meta 的首席财务官 Susan Li 表示：“代理将成为现实演变的重要组成部分，每个人都必须适应。”毕竟，Meta 表示，Muse 可能仍然对消费者免费，而企业则需要支付交易费用。
Meta 确实需要 Muse 才能发挥作用。该公司的资本支出激增，其他财务义务也不断增加。它计划在 2026 年支出 1,350 亿至 1,450 亿美元，是去年支出的两倍。截至昨天，陪审团认定该公司违反了新墨西哥州消费者保护法，该公司欠新墨西哥州 250 亿美元。 Meta 以及其他大型科技公司面临着越来越大的压力，需要证明其人工智能投资是值得的。
忘记消费者吧——目前尚不清楚 Meta 本身是否能负担得起其计划。扎克伯格在电话会议上明确表示，之所以没有在国际上推出 Muse，是因为计算效率。
以 Muses 网络所需的级别运行 GPU 非常昂贵且耗能，而 Meta 似乎已经达到了其当前数据中心运营所能实现的极限。扎克伯格告诉投资者，计划明年将其计算成本效率提高“10 倍”。他没有解释该公司计划如何做到这一点。幸运的是，对于他（可能还有我们其他人）来说，已经有研究表明数据中心如何通过能源使用策略最大化计算能力，同时减少电网压力。也许他会读。
最终，如果 Meta 无法弄清楚如何降低其计算成本，Muse 将无法盈利，也不会成功。扎克伯格自己也这么说。
“到目前为止，最大的限制之一是，由于这是一项需要运行的计算密集型服务，因此我们尚未在全球范围内推出它，”扎克伯格告诉一位投资者，当他询问他认为增长 Muse 用户群的“限制因素”时。
扎克伯格表示，考虑到 Muse 仅来自美国和加拿大，自推出以来的 1000 万次下载量更加令人印象深刻，并补充道，“如果我们真的更广泛地推广它，那么你会期望这个数字会比我们今天看到的要大得多。”
扎克伯格至少似乎明白，有些人——也许对他来说更重要的是一些企业——不会立即“理解”Muse。没关系，他说。 “我们将按照对他们有意义的条款与人们合作，”他说。 “我确实认为，随着时间的推移，这对每个人来说都非常有价值。”
话又说回来，这就是给你带来元宇宙的同一个人。我们会看看会发生什么。
